**1. Codify the hardened WAF Web ACL in infrastructure-as-code so the manual mitigation is durable and not reverted on the next deploy.**

The Web ACL config that allowed the attack through is pre-existing. Update the IaC/CDK template managing CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 to persist: (1) the rate-based rule with Action=Block + a scope-down excluding the authorized load-test IP set; (2) a malicious-IP block set + Block rule; (3) a sensitive-path URI blocklist. Re-evaluate the 300 req/5min threshold against measured legitimate per-IP peaks rather than leaving the CloudFront default.

Acceptance criteria:
- The rate-based rule is defined with Action Block (not Count) and a scope-down exclusion for authorized load generators.
- A malicious-IP block rule and a sensitive-path URI blocklist rule are present in the IaC and deploy within the WCU budget.
- A redeploy reproduces the hardened Web ACL exactly, with no drift back to the counting-only rate rule.

**2. Validate and strengthen injection coverage so SQLi/XSS is blocked by content inspection independent of User-Agent.**

During the incident the SQLi managed rule set recorded zero terminating blocks; sqlmap was stopped only because its User-Agent tripped CommonRuleSet BadBots_Header. A stealthier injection with a spoofed browser User-Agent may evade this. Review/tune AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet and CommonRuleSet coverage for query-string, body, and URI injection, add targeted rules or raise sensitivity, then confirm injection payloads are blocked when sent with a benign User-Agent.

Acceptance criteria:
- A SQLi/XSS payload sent with a spoofed benign browser User-Agent is blocked by injection/content inspection, not a bad-bot UA signature.

*Apply the hardened rule set in one update: rate rule P1 → Block with a NOT(IPSet exclusions) scope-down, a new P10 Block rule referencing the malicious-IP set, and a new P11 Block rule for sensitive recon URI paths, preserving all P0/P2/P3/P4/P5 managed groups.*

```bash

```

**1. Codify the hardened WAF Web ACL in infrastructure-as-code so the manual mitigation is durable and not reverted on the next deploy.**

The Web ACL config that allowed the attack through is pre-existing. Update the IaC/CDK template managing CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 to persist: (1) the rate-based rule with Action=Block + a scope-down excluding the authorized load-test IP set; (2) a malicious-IP block set + Block rule; (3) a sensitive-path URI blocklist. Re-evaluate the 300 req/5min threshold against measured legitimate per-IP peaks rather than leaving the CloudFront default.

Acceptance criteria:
- The rate-based rule is defined with Action Block (not Count) and a scope-down exclusion for authorized load generators.
- A malicious-IP block rule and a sensitive-path URI blocklist rule are present in the IaC and deploy within the WCU budget.
- A redeploy reproduces the hardened Web ACL exactly, with no drift back to the counting-only rate rule.

**2. Validate and strengthen injection coverage so SQLi/XSS is blocked by content inspection independent of User-Agent.**

During the incident the SQLi managed rule set recorded zero terminating blocks; sqlmap was stopped only because its User-Agent tripped CommonRuleSet BadBots_Header. A stealthier injection with a spoofed browser User-Agent may evade this. Review/tune AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet and CommonRuleSet coverage for query-string, body, and URI injection, add targeted rules or raise sensitivity, then confirm injection payloads are blocked when sent with a benign User-Agent.

Acceptance criteria:
- A SQLi/XSS payload sent with a spoofed benign browser User-Agent is blocked by injection/content inspection, not a bad-bot UA signature.
- The SQLiRuleSet (or an added injection rule) records terminating blocks for injection test traffic in CloudWatch WAF metrics/sampled requests.
- Coverage is verified for query string, request body, and URI path injection vectors.","children":[]}]}]}]}}

**1. Codify the hardened WAF Web ACL in infrastructure-as-code so the manual mitigation is durable and not reverted on the next deploy.**

The Web ACL config that allowed the attack through is pre-existing. Update the IaC/CDK template managing CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 to persist: (1) the rate-based rule with Action=Block + a scope-down excluding the authorized load-test IP set; (2) a malicious-IP block set + Block rule; (3) a sensitive-path URI blocklist. Re-evaluate the 300 req/5min threshold against measured legitimate per-IP peaks rather than leaving the CloudFront default.

Acceptance criteria:
- The rate-based rule is defined with Action Block (not Count) and a scope-down exclusion for authorized load generators.
- A malicious-IP block rule and a sensitive-path URI blocklist rule are present in the IaC and deploy within the WCU budget.
- A redeploy reproduces the hardened Web ACL exactly, with no drift back to the counting-only rate rule.

**2. Validate and strengthen injection coverage so SQLi/XSS is blocked by content inspection independent of User-Agent.**

During the incident the SQLi managed rule set recorded zero terminating blocks; sqlmap was stopped only because its User-Agent tripped CommonRuleSet BadBots_Header. A stealthier injection with a spoofed browser User-Agent may evade this. Review/tune AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet and CommonRuleSet coverage for query-string, body, and URI injection, add targeted rules or raise sensitivity, then confirm injection payloads are blocked when sent with a benign User-Agent.

Acceptance criteria:
- A SQLi/XSS payload sent with a spoofed benign browser User-Agent is blocked by injection/content inspection, not a bad-bot UA signature.
- The SQLiRuleSet (or an added injection rule) records terminating blocks for injection test traffic in CloudWatch WAF metrics/sampled requests.
- Coverage is verified for query string, request body, and URI path injection vectors.","children":[]}]}]}]}}

Codify the hardened WAF Web ACL in infrastructure-as-code so the manual mitigation is durable and not reverted on the next deploy.**\n\nThe Web ACL config that allowed the attack through is pre-existing. Update the IaC/CDK template managing CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 to persist: (1) the rate-based rule with Action=Block + a scope-down excluding the authorized load-test IP set; (2) a malicious-IP block set + Block rule; (3) a sensitive-path URI blocklist. Re-evaluate the 300 req/5min threshold against measured legitimate per-IP peaks rather than leaving the CloudFront default.\n\nAcceptance criteria:\n- The rate-based rule is defined with Action Block (not Count) and a scope-down exclusion for authorized load generators.\n- A malicious-IP block rule and a sensitive-path URI blocklist rule are present in the IaC and deploy within the WCU budget.\n- A redeploy reproduces the hardened Web ACL exactly, with no drift back to the counting-only rate rule.\n\n**2. Validate and strengthen injection coverage so SQLi/XSS is blocked by content inspection independent of User-Agent.**\n\nDuring the incident the SQLi managed rule set recorded zero terminating blocks; sqlmap was stopped only because its User-Agent tripped CommonRuleSet BadBots_Header. A stealthier injection with a spoofed browser User-Agent may evade this. Review/tune AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet and CommonRuleSet coverage for query-string, body, and URI injection, add targeted rules or raise sensitivity, then confirm injection payloads are blocked when sent with a benign User-Agent.\n\nAcceptance criteria:\n- A SQLi/XSS payload sent with a spoofed benign browser User-Agent is blocked by injection/content inspection, not a bad-bot UA signature.\n- The SQLiRuleSet (or an added injection rule) records terminating blocks for injection test traffic in CloudWatch WAF metrics/sampled requests.\n- Coverage is verified for query string, request body, and URI path injection vectors.","children":[]}]}]}]}}

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### WAF allowed 169,677 vs blocked only 250 requests
**Description:** Over the window WAF allowed 169,677 requests via Default_Action and blocked only 250 (~0.15%): 245 by CommonRuleSet and 5 by KnownBadInputs. The flood volume passed unblocked.
**Time:** 2026-10-10T17:00:00Z - 2026-10-10T18:15:00Z

### High-volume L7 HTTP flood from 198.51.100.10 (all allowed)
**Description:** Single source IP **198.51.100.10** (US) generated **168,126 ALLOWED** requests — ~99% of all traffic — at roughly **37 req/s sustained for 75 minutes**. Every request targeted **legitimate application paths** (`/cart`, `/catalog`, `/home`, `/checkout`, `/checkout/payment`, `/checkout/delivery`, product UUID pages), NOT exploit/recon URIs. This is a volumetric Layer-7 HTTP flood / load generator rather than an exploit scanner. All of it passed WAF because the per-IP rate-based rule (300/5min) is in **Count mode, not Block**.
**Time:** 2026-10-10T17:00:00Z - 2026-10-10T18:15:00Z

### Sensitive-file / path-traversal recon from 198.51.100.20 reached origin
**Description:** IP **198.51.100.20** (US) ran a broad sensitive-file / path-traversal reconnaissance sweep: hundreds of distinct recon URIs including `/.git/HEAD`, `/.git/config`, `/.env`, `/wp-login.php`, `/phpmyadmin/`, `/actuator/env`, `/actuator/heapdump`, `/.aws/credentials`, `/settings.py`, `/v2/api-docs`, and many `/backup/*`, `/old/*`, `/dev/*`, `/test/*` prefixed variants. The **majority of these recon requests were ALLOWED through to the EKS origin**; only a narrow set of `.env` / `.env.bak` / `web.config` / `wp-config.php.bak` / `.aws/credentials` variants were BLOCKED (RestrictedExtensions_URIPath). Reconnaissance largely reached origin.
**Time:** 2026-10-10T17:00:00Z

### Injection attacks from 198.51.100.60 against /catalog (all 225 blocked)
**Description:** IP **198.51.100.60** (US) launched classic injection attacks against `/catalog`: **LFI** (`file=../../../../etc/passwd`, `etc/shadow`), **XSS** (`search=<script>alert(1)</script>`, `javascript:alert(1)`), and **SQLi** (`id=1 UNION SELECT username,password FROM users--`). All **225 requests were BLOCKED** by AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet. This is the one actor the WAF managed rules fully stopped.
**Time:** 2026-10-10T17:00:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: Rate-based rule in Count mode let the single-source flood through
**Description:** The flood from 198.51.100.10 (~168k requests, well over the 300/5min threshold) was never blocked because AWS-RateBasedRule-IP-300 is set to Count, not Block. Generic signature rules caught only a 250-request trickle. Switching the rate rule to Block is the likely mitigation — pending confirmation of what the traffic actually was (flood vs. legitimate burst).
**Cascades to:** symptom-waf-mostly-allow, symptom-single-source-flood, symptom-recon-scanner

#### Supporting Observations
- **Top client IPs: 198.51.100.10 dominates:** 198.51.100.10 (US) ALLOW 168,126; 198.51.100.30 (US) ALLOW 1,351; 198.51.100.60 (US) BLOCK 225; 198.51.100.20 (US) ALLOW 200 / BLOCK 25. One IP accounts for ~99% of all allowed traffic — a volumetric pattern the Count-mode rate rule did not stop.
- **WAF action distribution: 169,677 ALLOW / 250 BLOCK:** Athena aggregation over default.waf_logs for the window. ALLOW 169,677 (Default_Action), BLOCK 250 (CommonRuleSet 245 + KnownBadInputs 5). Blocks were generic signature hits (BadBots_Header 225, RestrictedExtensions 15, GenericLFI 5, ExploitablePaths 5), not volumetric. The rate-based rule in Count mode never terminated any request.

### Cause: Card-testing burst did not create order/payment records
**Description:** The 1,350 POST /checkout/payment requests from 198.51.100.30 cleared the WAF edge but did NOT persist at the data layer (HIGH confidence): Aurora example-shop-orders and DynamoDB example-shop-carts show flat/baseline writes at 18:05 (see obs-orders-no-write-spike). No order/payment records were created; payment is very likely a mock path (retail-store-sample-app, medium-high confidence inference). No payment-processor fraud review or chargeback handling is warranted. This materially limits confirmed impact.
**Cascades to:** symptom-waf-mostly-allow

#### Supporting Observations
- **No order/payment write spike at 18:05 (card testing did not persist):** Aurora PostgreSQL example-shop-orders writer (example-shop-orders-one) and DynamoDB example-shop-carts write metrics are flat/baseline through 18:04-18:06, no spike at the 18:05 card-testing burst. CommitThroughput at 18:05 = 7.42 commits/s vs baseline 5.8-7.7; WriteIOPS 24.98 vs baseline 17.6-26.5; DatabaseConnections flat at 10; DynamoDB PutItem SampleCount 224 vs baseline 107-249. A real 1,350-INSERT burst would have driven commits to ~27+/s. Period 60s, window 2026-10-10T17:48-18:08Z, region us-west-2, account 012345678901_1.

#### Gaps
- **Origin HTTP outcomes for allowed recon are unrecoverable:** Whether the ~200 allowed recon probes (198.51.100.20) and 1,350 card-testing POSTs returned real data at the EKS origin cannot be confirmed from available telemetry. The incident-time HTTP origin LB appears DELETED/REPLACED: CloudFront's configured origin DNS (k8s-ui-ui-0000000001...) does not match the only existing LB (...-deed3f1375016a93), a Layer-4 NLB with HTTP access logging disabled that shows ZERO flow datapoints during the 2026-10-10 17:00-18:15 window but emits normally today (~40-52 flows/hr; 15-month metric retention rules out aging). EKS pod logs are inaccessible (example-shop CONFIG_MAP auth; principal not in aws-auth) and would be aged; Application Signals / aws/spans / X-Ray have no data in the window. The card-testing persistence question was answered via Aurora/DynamoDB write metrics instead (see obs-orders-no-write-spike). Remaining gaps: Performance Insights disabled (no per-statement SQL), no RDS log exports for example-shop-orders, no direct row count. Recon data exposure therefore remains UNDETERMINED — an access/data gap, not evidence of no impact. Onward avenues: CloudTrail UpdateDistribution history to identify the old LB; RDS audit log + orders datastore for order rows.

### Hypothesis: Recon traffic largely reached the origin
**Description:** Because the per-IP rate-based rule is in **Count mode** and the managed rule groups only block a narrow set of file extensions (`.env`, `.env.bak`, `web.config`, `wp-config.php.bak`, `.aws/credentials`), the bulk of 198.51.100.20's reconnaissance sweep — `/.git/HEAD`, `/actuator/env`, `/actuator/heapdump`, `/phpmyadmin/`, `/settings.py`, `/v2/api-docs`, and most `/backup/*` paths — was **served by the EKS origin** rather than blocked at the edge. Whether any of these recon probes returned sensitive content is not yet confirmed.
**Cascades to:** symptom-recon-scanner

#### Supporting Observations
- **Traffic resolves into four distinct actors:** Per-IP request-pattern breakdown shows the traffic is not one event but **four distinct actors**:

1. **198.51.100.10** — 168,126 ALLOWED requests to legitimate app paths (`/cart`, `/catalog`, `/home`, `/checkout/*`, product UUIDs). High-volume **L7 HTTP flood** (~37 req/s, 75 min).
2. **198.51.100.20** — hundreds of distinct GET recon URIs (`/.git`, `/.env`, `/actuator/env`, `/.aws/credentials`, `/wp-login.php`, `/phpmyadmin/`, `/backup/*`); **majority ALLOWED**, only a few extension-matched variants blocked. **Sensitive-file recon scanner**.
3. **198.51.100.60** — 225 BLOCKED GETs to `/catalog` with LFI/XSS/SQLi payloads. **Injection attacker, fully blocked** by CommonRuleSet.
4. **198.51.100.30** — 1,350 ALLOWED POSTs to `/checkout/payment`. **Checkout-POST source** (possible carding, lower confidence).

Summary: one flooder, one recon scanner, one blocked injection attacker, and one checkout-POST source.

#### Gaps
- **Origin HTTP outcomes for allowed recon are unrecoverable:** Whether the ~200 allowed recon probes (198.51.100.20) and 1,350 card-testing POSTs returned real data at the EKS origin cannot be confirmed from available telemetry. The incident-time HTTP origin LB appears DELETED/REPLACED: CloudFront's configured origin DNS (k8s-ui-ui-0000000001...) does not match the only existing LB (...-deed3f1375016a93), a Layer-4 NLB with HTTP access logging disabled that shows ZERO flow datapoints during the 2026-10-10 17:00-18:15 window but emits normally today (~40-52 flows/hr; 15-month metric retention rules out aging). EKS pod logs are inaccessible (example-shop CONFIG_MAP auth; principal not in aws-auth) and would be aged; Application Signals / aws/spans / X-Ray have no data in the window. The card-testing persistence question was answered via Aurora/DynamoDB write metrics instead (see obs-orders-no-write-spike). Remaining gaps: Performance Insights disabled (no per-statement SQL), no RDS log exports for example-shop-orders, no direct row count. Recon data exposure therefore remains UNDETERMINED — an access/data gap, not evidence of no impact. Onward avenues: CloudTrail UpdateDistribution history to identify the old LB; RDS audit log + orders datastore for order rows.
- **sqlmap run stopped by User-Agent signature, not injection inspection:** All 225 sqlmap payloads were blocked via CommonRuleSet BadBots_Header matching the `sqlmap/1.8.2` User-Agent (plus GenericLFI_URIPath), while the dedicated SQLiRuleSet recorded 0 terminating blocks. A spoofed/absent User-Agent carrying the same injection payloads could evade detection, since blocking relied on the tool's self-identifying UA rather than injection-specific request inspection.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Harden and contain the CloudFront WAF Web ACL CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 (CLOUDFRONT scope): (1) switch the rate-based rule AWS-RateBasedRule-IP-300-CreatedByCloudFront from Count to Block, scoped down to exclude the authorized load-test source; (2) add a dedicated IP set + high-priority Block rule for the three malicious source IPs; (3) add a URI-path blocklist Block rule for the sensitive recon patterns reaching origin.

## Reasoning
The Web ACL allowed significant malicious traffic because its rate-based rule only counted requests. Origin-side verification refines urgency: the 1,350 card-testing POSTs cleared the WAF edge but did NOT persist (flat writes in Aurora example-shop-orders and DynamoDB example-shop-carts; likely a mock payment path) — so no fraud/chargeback review is warranted and the Count→Block change is for abuse/cost prevention and future containment, not confirmed-fraud remediation. The ~200/225 recon probes that reached origin remain UNDETERMINED (origin HTTP outcomes unrecoverable). The sqlmap run was blocked only incidentally by its User-Agent. This is a security-posture hardening/containment change, fully reversible via the captured baseline.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the hardened WAF Web ACL configuration in IaC so the mitigation is durable.
**Description:** The Web ACL config that allowed the attack through is pre-existing. Update the IaC/CDK template managing CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 to persist: (1) the rate-based rule with Action=Block + a scope-down excluding the authorized load-test IP set; (2) a malicious-IP block set + Block rule; (3) a sensitive-path URI blocklist. Re-evaluate the 300 req/5min threshold against measured legitimate per-IP peaks rather than leaving the CloudFront default.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The rate-based rule is defined with Action Block (not Count) and a scope-down exclusion for authorized load generators.
- A malicious-IP block rule and a sensitive-path URI blocklist rule are present in the IaC definition and deploy within the WCU budget.
- A redeploy reproduces the hardened Web ACL exactly, with no drift back to the counting-only rate rule.

#### 2. Validate and strengthen injection coverage so SQLi/XSS is blocked by content inspection independent of User-Agent.
**Description:** During the incident the SQLi managed rule set recorded zero terminating blocks; sqlmap was stopped only because its User-Agent tripped CommonRuleSet BadBots_Header. A stealthier injection with a spoofed browser User-Agent may evade this. Review/tune AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet and CommonRuleSet coverage for query-string, body, and URI injection, add targeted rules or raise sensitivity, then confirm injection payloads are blocked when sent with a benign User-Agent.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- A SQLi/XSS payload sent with a spoofed benign browser User-Agent is blocked by content inspection, not a bad-bot UA signature.
- The SQLiRuleSet (or an added injection rule) records terminating blocks for injection test traffic.
- Coverage is verified for query string, request body, and URI path vectors.

#### 3. Close the origin-side observability gap so future edge-cleared traffic has a recoverable origin outcome.
**Description:** The ~200 recon probe outcomes were unrecoverable (incident-time HTTP origin LB deleted/replaced, current LB is an L4 NLB with access logging disabled, EKS pod logs inaccessible, X-Ray/Application Signals empty for the window). Enable CloudFront access logging on distribution EEXAMPLE000001 and ALB access logs at the origin, and retain EKS ui request logs, so a future recon or injection run that clears the WAF can be assessed for actual data exposure.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- CloudFront access logging (standard or real-time) is enabled for distribution EEXAMPLE000001 with a retained log destination.
- Origin request/response status codes are captured and retained (ALB access logs or equivalent) for the origin serving the ui service.
- A test request to a sensitive path can be traced end-to-end to its origin HTTP status in the logs.
